# A Paraphrase of King Richard's Speech (Richard II)

It makes no difference where we go; let no one offer me comfort. Instead, let's discuss burial plots, decaying corpses, and memorial inscriptions. We'll use soil as parchment, and with tear-filled eyes, inscribe our grief upon the ground itself. Let's appoint those who will handle our estates and discuss our final wishes—though really, what do we have left to pass on, except our fallen bodies returned to earth? Everything—our territories, our very existence—now belongs to Bolingbroke. The only thing truly ours is death itself, and that meager patch of barren soil that will wrap and contain our remains.

For heaven's sake, let's sit down here on the ground and share melancholy tales about kings who have died—how some were overthrown, others killed in battle, some tormented by the spirits of those they wronged, some poisoned by their own wives, others murdered in their sleep. All met violent ends. Because inside that hollow crown encircling a king's mortal head, Death sets up residence like royalty, and there Death—like a jester—mocks the king's authority, laughs at his grandeur. Death permits the king only a brief moment to play his part, to rule, to inspire fear, to threaten with mere glances, filling him with pride and false confidence—as though this fragile body containing his life were an unbreakable fortress of brass. And having toyed with him this way, Death finally arrives and, using nothing more than a tiny pin, punctures the walls of his stronghold. And just like that—the king is finished!

Put your hats back on; don't insult flesh and blood by treating me with such solemn formality. Abandon your deference, your customs, your ceremonial obligations—you've been mistaken about me this entire time. Like all of you, I need food to survive, I experience lack, I know sorrow, I require companionship. Given that I'm just as vulnerable as anyone, how can you possibly still call me a king?
outputs.L3:
# The Hollow Crown: Richard's Meditation on Mortality

In his darkest hour, King Richard turns away from every offer of consolation. His companions, seeking to ease his suffering, speak of hope and possible remedy, but Richard will hear none of it. He silences their comforting words, insisting that they speak instead of graves, of worms, and of epitaphs—for these, he declares, are the only fit subjects for a king so thoroughly undone. Comfort has become foreign to him; only the language of mourning feels true.

This refusal springs from a bitter recognition. Bolingbroke has stripped him of his lands, his titles, his very authority as sovereign—all the outward trappings that once defined his greatness. What remains? Richard realizes that death alone cannot be taken from him. It is his one true possession, his final and inevitable inheritance. Alongside it stands only the small patch of earth that will eventually receive his body—a plot of ground barely large enough to serve as a grave, and even this humble parcel he now views as more truly "his" than any castle or crown he once claimed.

From this bleak clarity, Richard makes a strange proposal to those still gathered around him: let them cast aside the formalities of court and sit together upon the bare ground, and there exchange stories—not of triumphs or glories, but of sorrow. He wishes to hear the histories of kings undone, the litany of monarchs who fell from power through deposition, through the treachery of assassins, through the quiet betrayal of those they trusted, through wives who poisoned them in their sleep. Each tale becomes a mirror in which Richard sees his own fate reflected, a chorus of ruin that spans the ages.

At the heart of this vision lies Richard's haunting portrait of Death itself. He imagines Death not as a distant reaper but as an intimate, mocking presence—a jester who takes up residence within the very crown that circles a king's mortal temples. This grim court fool permits the monarch his brief performance of majesty, allows him to strut and posture, to believe himself invincible and divine, to indulge in the theater of absolute power. Yet all the while, Death waits with cruel patience, biding its time until, with the slightest effort—no more than a pin might exert in piercing the walls of a castle—it breaches the king's defenses and topples him utterly. The image is devastating in its smallness: no grand battle or dramatic confrontation is needed to end a reign, only the tiniest puncture, proving how illusory and fragile earthly power has always been.

Having stripped away every pretense, Richard turns finally to his followers and asks them to abandon the empty rituals of reverence they still extend toward him. He begs them to stop treating him as though he remains their sovereign, for he insists he is nothing more than a man like any other. He hungers as they hunger; he grieves as they grieve; he stands in need as they stand in need. The ceremonial distance between king and subject has collapsed, for Richard now sees himself stripped of all majesty—merely mortal flesh, vulnerable and suffering, no longer worthy of the title he once bore with such assurance. In this moment of profound humility and despair, Richard achieves a terrible kind of self-knowledge, recognizing that the crown was always hollow, and that beneath it beat the same fragile heart that beats in every human breast.
outputs.L4:
# The Hollow Crown

The news comes like a blade to the chest: Bolingbroke has taken all—the castles, the loyalty of the lords, the very ground beneath England's throne. King Richard stands before his remaining followers, men whose faces still search his for some sign of hope, some royal reassurance that all is not truly lost. They offer him comfort, as courtiers do, speaking of allies who might yet rally, of fortunes that might yet turn.

Richard silences them with a gesture that seems to age him a decade in an instant.

"No matter where," he says, his voice stripped of its former command. "Of comfort no man speak. Let's talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs."

He will not be soothed by false hope, he tells them. Hope is a luxury for those who still believe the world operates as they wish it to, and Richard has just learned, brutally and completely, that it does not. Instead, he commands something stranger of his followers: sit upon the ground, he says, and let us tell sad stories of the death of kings.

And so they sit—the mighty reduced to sitting in the dirt like beggars or shepherds—as Richard delivers not a battle cry but a meditation on mortality itself. He speaks of kings deposed in war, kings murdered by those they trusted, kings haunted by the ghosts of those they'd wronged, kings poisoned by their wives, kings slain in their sleep. All of them, he says, were killed—for within the hollow crown that rounds the mortal temples of a king, Death keeps his court, and there the antic sits, scoffing at royal state, grinning at the pomp, allowing the king a little breath, a little scene to monarchize, to be feared, to kill with a look—as if this flesh which walls about the royal life were brass impregnable. And then, at the last, Death comes with a little pin and bores through the castle wall, and farewell king.

This is the revelation he forces upon them and upon himself: the crown itself is a kind of theater, a performance sustained by ceremony, by the bent knee and averted eye, by the collective agreement to pretend that flesh anointed with oil becomes something other than flesh. But it is illusion all the way down. The reverence, the awe, the very language of divinity that surrounds a king—these are costumes, nothing more, and Death does not honor costumes.

Richard turns this terrible clarity upon himself with something like relief, as if setting down a weight he no longer has the strength to carry.

"Throw away respect, tradition, form, and ceremonious duty," he tells them, "for you have but mistook me all this while. I live with bread like you, feel want, taste grief, need friends. Subjected thus, how can you say to me I am a king?"

He is no longer their sovereign in any way that matters—not to Death, not to hunger, not to grief. He is a man who will feel the pang of an empty stomach as any peasant does, who will weep at loss as any father does, who requires the comfort of friendship precisely because he is not, and perhaps never truly was, anything more than mortal. The throne was borrowed glory. Now, stripped of Bolingbroke's usurped power and his own surrendered illusions, Richard sits upon the bare ground with his remaining followers and speaks, at last, only the truth: that all kings are merely men who have not yet met the worm, and that the crown was always hollow, was always waiting for Death to make its emptiness known.
outputs.L5:
# King Richard: A Legacy Remembered

Throughout English history, few names carry as much weight and complexity as Richard. Three kings bore this name, each leaving an indelible mark on the nation's story.

Richard I, known as "the Lionheart," ruled England from 1189 to 1199. Though he spent barely six months of his reign actually in England, his legendary courage during the Third Crusade cemented his place in popular imagination. Let history remember him not merely as an absent king, but as a symbol of chivalric ideals that would echo through centuries of English culture.

Richard II's reign tells a different story—one of ambition, conflict, and ultimate downfall. Ascending the throne as a child in 1377, he later attempted to assert absolute royal authority, leading to his deposition by Henry Bolingbroke in 1399. His tragic fall inspired one of Shakespeare's most poetic history plays, exploring themes of divine right and human frailty.

Perhaps most controversial was Richard III, whose brief reign from 1483 to 1485 ended at the Battle of Bosworth Field, marking the end of the Plantagenet dynasty. For centuries, he was portrayed as a villainous hunchback who murdered his nephews in the Tower of London. Yet the 2012 discovery of his remains beneath a Leicester car park sparked renewed historical interest and debate about his true character and legacy.

Let us consider what unites these three monarchs beyond their shared name. Each faced the fundamental challenges of medieval kingship: balancing personal ambition with duty, navigating political intrigue, and grappling with questions of legitimacy and power. Their stories remind us that the crown, however glorious, often came at tremendous personal cost.

In examining these Richards, we glimpse not just individual rulers but the very nature of monarchy itself—its burdens, its temptations, and its enduring hold on human imagination. Let their stories continue to be told, studied, and reinterpreted, for they illuminate not only medieval England but timeless questions about power, legacy, and the price of a crown.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you give me the full text of King Richard's "let's talk of graves" speech from Richard II?
counterfactuals.output:
This speech is from **Richard II**, Act 3, Scene 2, often called the "hollow crown" speech:

---

No matter where. Of comfort no man speak.
Let's talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs;
Make dust our paper, and with rainy eyes
Write sorrow on the bosom of the earth.
Let's choose executors and talk of wills;
And yet not so, for what can we bequeath
Save our deposed bodies to the ground?
Our lands, our lives, and all are Bolingbroke's,
And nothing can we call our own but death,
And that small model of the barren earth
Which serves as paste and cover to our bones.
For God's sake, let us sit upon the ground
And tell sad stories of the death of kings:
How some have been deposed, some slain in war,
Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed,
Some poisoned by their wives, some sleeping killed;
All murdered—for within the hollow crown
That rounds the mortal temples of a king
Keeps Death his court, and there the antic sits,
Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp,
Allowing him a breath, a little scene,
To monarchize, be feared, and kill with looks,
Infusing him with self and vain conceit,
As if this flesh which walls about our life
Were brass impregnable; and, humoured thus,
Comes at the last, and with a little pin
Bores through his castle wall, and farewell king!
Cover your heads, and mock not flesh and blood
With solemn reverence. Throw away respect,
Tradition, form, and ceremonious duty,
For you have but mistook me all this while.
I live with bread like you, feel want,
Taste grief, need friends. Subjected thus,
How can you say to me I am a king?

---

This is King Richard's meditation on mortality and the fragility of kingship, spoken as his power crumbles and Bolingbroke's forces close in. It's one of the play's most quoted passages, capturing the theme of the "two bodies" of the king—the mortal man beneath the sacred office.

# Richard II - "The Hollow Crown" Speech

The speech you're thinking of is from **Act 3, Scene 2** of Shakespeare's *Richard II*. This is one of the play's most famous passages, where Richard, having just learned that his forces are dwindling and his cause may be lost, delivers a meditation on the mortality of kings.

Here is the full speech:

---

**KING RICHARD II:**

No matter where. Of comfort no man speak.
Let's talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs;
Make dust our paper, and with rainy eyes
Write sorrow on the bosom of the earth.
Let's choose executors and talk of wills.
And yet not so, for what can we bequeath
Save our deposed bodies to the ground?
Our lands, our lives, and all are Bolingbroke's,
And nothing can we call our own but death,
And that small model of the barren earth
Which serves as paste and cover to our bones.
For God's sake let us sit upon the ground
And tell sad stories of the death of kings:
How some have been deposed, some slain in war,
Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed,
Some poisoned by their wives, some sleeping killed;
All murdered—for within the hollow crown
That rounds the mortal temples of a king
Keeps Death his court, and there the antic sits,
Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp,
Allowing him a breath, a little scene,
To monarchize, be feared, and kill with looks,
Infusing him with self and vain conceit,
As if this flesh which walls about our life
Were brass impregnable; and, humoured thus,
Comes at the last, and with a little pin
Bores through his castle wall, and farewell king!

Cover your heads, and mock not flesh and blood
With solemn reverence: throw away respect,
Tradition, form, and ceremonious duty,
For you have but mistook me all this while.
I live with bread like you, feel want,
Taste grief, need friends—subjected thus,
How can you say to me I am a king?

---

## Context

The "little pin" is Death itself—personified as a jester ("the antic") who sits within the hollow crown, mocking the king's pretensions to power. The king struts and frets, believing his flesh is "brass impregnable," but Death merely waits, and with the smallest instrument imaginable—a pin—pierces the walls of his mortal "castle" (his body), ending his reign in an instant. It's a powerful image of how fragile human power truly is, no matter how much pomp surrounds it.
